clue.text: An instruction for TLS staff that encompasses all aspects of text production

definitions.text: An instruction for TLS staff that encompasses all aspects of text production

parts.words: An instruction for TLS staff that encompasses all aspects of text production
parts.note: read as an order to a literary paper's staff, it tells them to put arts and ideas into type; read as a phrase, it names the whole world of books, printing and reading

explanation.surface: A memo to the Times Literary Supplement's staff covering every stage of making a text.
explanation.walkthrough: The TLS reviews books and the arts, so an instruction to its staff could be to put culture into print; the same two words are the academic term for the world shaped by printing.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a scholarly term for the society and practices built around printed books, from typesetting to reading.

clue.text: Perhaps the wrong person's gothic novel — a volume put in bin

parts.note: Rebecca is Daphne du Maurier's gothic novel of Manderley

indicators.note: put in says the article and the volume letter go inside the word for bin

parts.note: to ditch something is to bin it, throw it away

explanation.surface: Someone's dark romantic novel is a waste: one volume is thrown in the bin.
explanation.walkthrough: Rebecca Davitch is the heroine of Anne Tyler's Back When We Were Grownups, who opens the novel feeling she has turned into the wrong person; 'Perhaps' marks the definition as a hint rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Tyler's heroine famously discovers at fifty-three that she has become someone she was never meant to be.

clue.text: Christie's work with singular standards

parts.note: N or M? is an Agatha Christie novel featuring Tommy and Tuppence
S is the grammatical abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A Christie novel combined with a singular set of standards.
explanation.walkthrough: Agatha Christie's N or M? (1941) is a Tommy and Tuppence spy story; its title spelt without spaces is NORM.
explanation.definitionFit: Norms are accepted benchmarks of behaviour or quality, just as standards are.

clue.text: Camilla and Marge going without a dance in poetic imagery

indicators.note: going without says one letter of the names is dropped from the pool of letters
a dance moves the remaining letters of the two names about into a new order

explanation.surface: Two women, Camilla and Marge, sit out a dance in a poem full of pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going without' takes one A from CAMILLAMARGE, and 'dance' rearranges the other eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A calligram is a poem whose words are laid out to form a picture of its subject, as in Apollinaire's work.

clue.text: Deliver holiday travel

parts.note: leave is time off work, a holiday, as in annual leave
to go is to travel

explanation.surface: Bring the goods for a trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a dialect form of 'let go', used in the sense of setting free.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver is to release or set free, as in 'deliver us from evil', which matches releasing one's grip.

clue.text: Employmentin circuses

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the word circuses

explanation.walkthrough: The clue as published runs 'Employment' and 'in' together; 'in' is the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Employment of a tool or method is its use, the act of putting it to work.

clue.text: "Farewell: you shall find me in —" (Henry IV Part 1)

definitions.text: "Farewell: you shall find me in —" (Henry IV Part 1)

parts.words: "Farewell: you shall find me in —" (Henry IV Part 1)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Prince Hal's parting words to Falstaff name the London street where the Boar's Head tavern stood

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's history play with the place name left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Eastcheap is a street in the City of London, setting of the Boar's Head tavern where Falstaff drinks in the Henry IV plays.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank is filled by the London street that Prince Hal names as his meeting place in Act 2 of the play.

clue.text: A knight who's villainous and vile — he's a grocer in disguise

indicators.note: in disguise says these words appear with their letters rearranged

parts.note: the apostrophe drops out, leaving the three letters as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wicked knight is really a shopkeeper going about incognito.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Giles Overreach is the grasping, ruthless villain of Philip Massinger's comedy A New Way to Pay Old Debts.
explanation.definitionFit: Massinger's character is a knight whose extortion and cruelty make him the play's villain.

clue.text: Pitch including a bit of belaying, which helps many to ascend in the Alps

definitions.text: which helps many to ascend in the Alps

indicators.note: including says the pitch word holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: pitch is the black sticky substance tar

indicators.note: a bit of here takes only the first letter of belaying

explanation.surface: A climber's pitch, partly secured by belaying, is something many use to get up an Alpine slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' and 'belaying' paint a rock climb, but the answer is a ski lift; a T-bar tows skiers uphill with a bar behind them.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski tow pulls skiers up the slope on a T-shaped bar, carrying many uphill in the Alps.

clue.text: A change of direction for our subscribers or management

indicators.note: a change of direction swaps right for left, so the letter for right becomes the letter for left

parts.note: a paper's subscribers make up its readership

explanation.surface: Our paper's editors want a new course for subscribers or for its bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our' is the TLS speaking of its own readers; R (right) becomes L (left), the change of direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Leadership is the group of people who run an organisation, its management.

clue.text: A book on desire is taking off

parts.note: Acts of the Apostles is a book of the New Testament
to like something is to want it, as in 'I'd like that'

explanation.surface: A biblical book on longing is preparing to fly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking off' means imitating, not leaving the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking someone off is mimicking them, which is behaving in imitation of them.

clue.text: Victorian detective's reluctant response to a trend, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly says the phrase is heard rather than read, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: someone unwilling to follow fashion says 'buck it', as in bucking the trend

explanation.surface: A Victorian detective grudgingly reacts to the latest fashion, so we are told.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Bucket is the police detective in Dickens's Bleak House, one of the first detectives in English fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Inspector Bucket of Bleak House is a Victorian fictional detective.

clue.text: Grim eastern beasts rampaging in Kipling's work for children

indicators.note: rampaging says the letters are rearranged wildly

explanation.surface: Fearsome animals from the East run riot in a Kipling story for the young.
explanation.walkthrough: Big Steamers is Kipling's poem for children about the cargo ships that feed Britain, from his History of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling wrote this poem for a children's history book, so it is one of his works for young readers.

clue.text: Tenor apt to play around with G & S operetta showpiece

indicators.note: to play around with something is to fiddle with it, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tenor fits nicely when he improvises in a Gilbert and Sullivan piece.
explanation.walkthrough: G & S is Gilbert and Sullivan; their tongue-twisting fast numbers, such as the Major-General's song, are the classic example.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapid comic song packed with words is a showpiece of Gilbert and Sullivan operettas.

clue.text: Fool seen with the French king — one replaced by the French Hamlet?

parts.note: a tit is a fool, a silly person

indicators.note: replaced by says the letter for one is swapped out for the French article

parts.note: le roi is French for the king
the Roman numeral for one is I
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A jester alongside the King of France, with one replaced by a French Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: In LE ROI the I is replaced by LE, giving LEROLE; the question mark marks Hamlet as an example, the part that names its play.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is the lead part named in the play's title, a famous example of such a role.

clue.text: Nero scene features this supporter of a Roman ruler

definitions.text: this supporter of a Roman ruler

indicators.note: features says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A scene involving Nero includes a loyal follower of a Roman leader.
explanation.walkthrough: Eros is Antony's faithful servant in Antony and Cleopatra, who kills himself rather than kill his master; Nero is a decoy emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's play Eros is the devoted attendant of Mark Antony, one of Rome's triumvirs.

clue.text: Scandalous Sheba's passion in conversation

indicators.note: in conversation says the word is spoken, giving one that sounds the same

parts.note: the heart is the seat of passion and strong feeling

explanation.surface: An outrageous Sheba's ardour, as discussed.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheba Hart is the teacher in Zoë Heller's novel Notes on a Scandal, hence 'Scandalous Sheba'.
explanation.definitionFit: The teacher at the centre of Zoë Heller's Notes on a Scandal is named Sheba Hart.

clue.text: Victim of a scheme to exploit farmland, written about by Dickens

parts.note: a mark is the target of a con or swindle
to tap a resource is to exploit it
a ley is land temporarily under grass, part of a farm

explanation.surface: Someone duped in a plan to make money from fields, as described by Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark Tapley is Martin Chuzzlewit's cheerful servant who goes with him to the swampy American settlement of Eden, sold to them in a land swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens created the ever-jolly servant in Martin Chuzzlewit, so the character is someone he wrote about.

clue.text: Some theatrical performances allowed? England's satisfied

parts.note: rep is short for repertory, a theatre presenting a run of plays
let means allowed

explanation.surface: Are some stage shows permitted? The English are content.
explanation.definitionFit: Being replete is being full after eating, so satisfied.

clue.text: Famous writer's poem "If"is rejected — remove it from book copy

indicators.note: rejected says the short word is turned back to front

parts.note: dele is the proofreader's mark telling the printer to delete something

explanation.surface: A celebrated author's poem 'If' is turned down and struck from the manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If' suggests Kipling, but the famous writer is Shakespeare: Fidele is the dirge 'Fear no more the heat o' the sun' from Cymbeline, often anthologised under that name.
explanation.definitionFit: The song sung over the disguised Imogen in Cymbeline is printed in anthologies with this title, a poem by Shakespeare.

clue.text: Devastated farm plot crossed by legions at Waterloo

indicators.note: something devastated is wrecked, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A ruined plot of farmland trampled by armies at the battle of Waterloo.
explanation.walkthrough: Waterloo suggests Napoleon's battlefield, but it is the busy London railway station, whose platforms crowds of commuters cross.
explanation.definitionFit: A station platform is walked across by huge numbers of travellers each day at a busy terminus.

clue.text: Possibly funny-sounding feature of Omar Kkayyam's poetry

indicators.note: sounding says the word is heard, giving one spelt differently

parts.note: farcy, from farce, would be a word for comically absurd

explanation.surface: Perhaps a comic-sounding aspect of the Rubáiyát.
explanation.walkthrough: Omar Khayyam wrote his quatrains in Persian; Farsi is its name for itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Persian is the language of the Rubáiyát, so the language is a defining characteristic of the poems.

clue.text: Bad outcome from a scrap or larger part of Anita Brookner's work

definitions.meaning: a fight can leave someone with an eye swollen shut

explanation.surface: A black eye from a fight, or most of a Brookner novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'or larger part of' links the two senses; a scrap here is a fight, not a fragment.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye swollen shut is a typical injury from a fistfight, and the phrase is also a Brookner title.

clue.text: An objective voice in command at last

indicators.note: at last takes the final letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: A goal stated in a commanding tone at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An end is an aim or goal, as in 'means to an end'.

clue.text: English enthralled by excellent American poet

indicators.note: enthralled by says the English letter is held inside the slang word

parts.note: rad is American slang for excellent

explanation.surface: The English captivated by a splendid American poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Herbert Read was an English poet and critic of art and literature.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Herbert Read wrote war poetry and criticism, so he is a poet.

clue.text: English tends to be oblique in Christie's work

indicators.note: oblique means slanting or indirect, so the letters are knocked out of their straight order

explanation.surface: English is inclined to be indirect in an Agatha Christie novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Endless Night (1967) is a late Agatha Christie novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie wrote the 1967 psychological thriller of this title.
